name: Sorbian
catalog_quote: StressTyp2 passage 1819 (Dogil forthc.): 'Main stress in Sorbian falls on the initial syllable and is realized phonetically by rising or higher pitch. Secondary stress is realized on the penultimate syllable in words containing four syllables or more. It is realized by lengthening the prominent syllable. Rhythmic stress is weak.' Mucke 1891:148 §82.1: 'Im Sorbischen wird wie im Čechischen ganz allgemein…

audit.recode_to: No recode of the rule; retire/merge the family-node record into the child records. The StressTyp2 lect's coordinates, grammars and example words are Lower Sorbian, and its rule string is identical to the catalog's lowe1385 record (10 100 1010 10010...), so lowe1385 is the natural merge target; uppe1395 (fixed-dominant, no secondary) stays separate. If the merge desk keeps a note: Mucke 1891:148 and Kaulfürst 2019 put the (optional, lengthening) penult Nebenton on words of THREE or more syllables in Lower Sorbian, against Dogil/Gordon-Janaš 'four or more' encoded as '100' for trisyllables.

sources.quote: "In general, primary stress always falls on the first syllable (e.g. wysoke ['wɨsokə] 'high neut'.) and its phonetic realization is a rising or higher pitch on the stressed syllable. ... Secondary stress is also assigned to the penultimate syllable in words with four or more syllables (e.g. beletrija ['beleˌtʰʁ̥ia] 'fiction'). sources.quote: Upper Sorbian traditionally described as fixed initial stress with rare exceptions (Šewc-Schuster 1984); 15-min Praat pilot of read speech finds strong lengthening of all unstressed phrase-final syllables; concludes it is wrong to posit a special secondary stress in trisyllables; stress correlates in Upper Sorbian not yet specifically investigated.

sources.citation: Kaulfürst 2019 'Akcent w słowje' pp.8-10 as summarised on niedersorbisch.de/dolnoserbski.de 'Betonung' page (held under sibling dir lowe1385)
sources.quote: Lower Sorbian: main stress on the first syllable of native words (also on negation particles and prefixes); in three- and more-syllable words a secondary accent can occur on the penult, its realisation optional; compounds and loans behave specially.

sources.citation: Mucke, Karl Ernst. 1891. Historische und vergleichende Laut- und Formenlehre der niedersorbischen (niederlausitzisch-wendischen) Sprache. Leipzig: Hirzel. (already; page 148 re-rendered, not newly fetched sources)
sources.quote: 82.1 Hauptton: every word stressed on the first syllable however many syllables. 82.2 Nebenton: in most regions of Lower Sorbian (and Muskau, partly the eastern border dialect) three- and more-syllable words carry a secondary stress on the penult, realised as lengthening, clearer the longer the word (ex. cerwjony, Lubosćański, powołanje, podrožnikojstwo). 82.3: in this Lower Sorbian is the bridge from Czech and Upper Sorbian to Polish; further east the Nebenton can even outrank the Hauptton.
